questions.knowledge_point: Solving First-Order Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=7.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-4x})}^{′}+4(u{e}^{-4x}) & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x}+4u{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}}+\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 7{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y=2x-5.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{x})}^{′}-(u{e}^{x}) & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}-u{e}^{x} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x}+\cancel{u{e}^{x}}-\cancel{u{e}^{x}} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x}(2x-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x}(2x-5) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{x} \\  & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{6x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{6x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{6x})}^{′}-6(u{e}^{6x}) & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x}+6u{e}^{6x}-6u{e}^{6x} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x}+\cancel{6u{e}^{6x}}-\cancel{6u{e}^{6x}} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{6x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{6x} \\  & =x{e}^{6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x=\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =3+3{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3+3{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3+3{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =3x{e}^{3x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$
